title: Marketing Is Not Failing. It Is Misplaced.
content:
The scene is familiar in many leadership meetings. The quarter is behind plan. Someone asks what marketing is doing about it. The answer arrives quickly: a new campaign, a larger media budget, more content, a promotion to lift the numbers. Activity rises. For a while, results may even improve. Then the same pressure returns, and with it the same conversation, now with a little more frustration on every side.

Sales says the leads are weak. Marketing says sales is not converting. Finance asks why spending keeps increasing while margins do not. Everyone is working hard, and yet the organization seems to be running in place.

In my experience, this pattern rarely means that marketing people lack talent or effort. More often, it means that marketing has been given the wrong job, and placed too late in the decisions that matter.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗿𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝗮𝘀𝗸

Most organizations regularly ask whether marketing is performing. Very few ask whether marketing is in the right place.

In many companies, the decisions that shape growth are made first: which customers to serve, what to offer, how to price it and what to promise. Marketing receives those decisions afterward, with an instruction to communicate them and generate demand. Its work is then judged by campaigns, content and leads.

In that arrangement, marketing has been classified as promotion: a downstream function that amplifies choices it had little chance to shape. Promotion is valuable. But when it becomes the whole job, the organization loses something far more important: market evidence at the moment decisions are made.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗺𝗶𝘀𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁𝘀

The cost of a misplaced marketing function rarely appears as a single line on a dashboard. It shows up as a series of familiar symptoms:

• Discounting becomes a habit. When the value of an offer is not clear to customers, price is left to do the persuading, and discounts become the default way to close.

• Promises outrun proof. Messages grow louder, but the evidence that makes them believable does not grow with them.

• Evidence arrives too late. Customer objections, reasons for switching and complaints about the experience exist inside the organization. They simply do not reach the people deciding until the decision has already been made.

• Blame replaces learning. When results disappoint, each function points to another, because no one
owned the decision that caused the problem.

Each of these looks like an execution problem. Each is usually a symptom of the same upstream cause: decisions made without timely market evidence, and a marketing function asked to fix the consequences afterward.

𝗔 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗰𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

The alternative is not to give marketing control over every decision. It is to reclassify marketing as governed strategic intelligence: the system that brings market reality into the decisions that shape what an organization offers, prices, promises and scales.

In practice, that system works as one connected loop:

• Sense brings market reality into the organization as evidence leaders can act on, not opinion.

• Shape turns that evidence into value choices: who to serve, what to offer, how to price and what to prove.

• Scale makes aligned value known and chosen, through channels, sales and digital media.

• Experience tests the promise against what customers actually receive, and returns that learning to the start of the loop.

Other functions keep their responsibilities. Finance still approves prices and investments. Operations still delivers. Sales still sells. What changes is that market evidence enters these decisions before they are locked, and someone is accountable for making sure it does.

𝗔 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝘄𝗲𝗲𝗸

You do not need a restructuring to see where your organization stands. Take the last three significant decisions your leadership team made about your priority customers, your pricing, your value proposition or the customer experience. For each one, ask two questions:

• Did market intelligence enter before the decision was locked?

• Could it have materially changed the decision?

If the answer to either question is no, marketing is still operating downstream in your organization, whatever the organization chart says.

Then go one step further. Who owned each decision? What evidence did they see, and was it specific to that decision or a general market update? What would have needed to be different for that evidence to change the outcome? The answers will tell you more about your growth problem than another campaign report.
title2: Putting marketing back where it belongs
content2:
The answer to stalled growth is not always more marketing, and it is certainly not less. It is marketing in the right place.

Promotion still matters. Its proper role, however, is to amplify value that is already clear, proven and deliverable, not to compensate for decisions made without understanding the market. When market evidence reaches decisions in time, discounting becomes a choice rather than a habit, promises are backed by proof, and growth becomes something leadership can govern rather than chase.

That is the shift from promotion to governed strategic intelligence. It begins with one simple discipline: decide with the market, not about it.
summary: When growth stalls, organizations ask marketing to do more. The deeper problem is often where marketing sits, and when it is allowed to influence decisions.

author_byline: By M. Q. Siddiqui, Founder, Siddiqui.digital
pull_quote: The problem is not poor marketing. It is misplaced marketing.
concluding_insight: Before asking marketing to do more, ask whether market evidence is reaching your most important decisions in time. If it is not, the problem is not the campaign. It is the classification.

title: SID Insights: bulk import of 35 articles
content:
SID Insights: bulk import of 35 articles

Please load these 35 articles directly into the blog database, instead of entering them through the admin panel.

Files

  • `articles.json`: all 35 articles (recommended source).
  • `articles.csv`: the same data as a spreadsheet, if easier.
  • `images/cover/`: cover image per article (1600 x 900, no text, crop-safe). Use as the article cover / card image.
  • `images/social/`: share image per article (1600 x 820, with title). Use for og:image / twitter:image.
  • `images/instagram/`: 1080 x 1350 images (for the author's Instagram; no website use needed).
  • `preview_first_two.html`: open in a browser to see how the body HTML should look.

Image file names match each article's `slug`.

Fields (one object per article)

| Field | Use |

|---|---|

| order | Publishing order (1 = oldest) |

| title, slug | Headline and URL: /blogs/{slug} |

| primary_category, secondary_categories | Use the existing category names exactly |

| author_byline, reading_time | As shown |

| standfirst | Short introduction under the headline |

| card_excerpt | Text on the blog cards and search results |

| body_html | Full article body as clean HTML (`<p>`, `<h2>`, `<ul><li>`, `<strong>`). No title or standfirst inside. |

| body_markdown | Same body in Markdown (`##` headings, `-` bullets), if the body is stored as Markdown |

| pull_quote, pull_quote_attribution | Pull quote has no quotation marks (the template adds them). Please show the attribution without a dash. |

| concluding_insight | Highlight panel at the end |

| cover_image, cover_image_alt | Cover image path and alt text |

| social_image | Use for og:image and twitter:image on this article page |

| display_date | Publication date to display (YYYY-MM-DD). Back-catalog dates are intentional. |

| status | `published` (date on or before 26 Oct 2026) or `scheduled` (publish automatically on display_date) |

| featured | true only for article 1 |

| show_book_panel | false for now (turn on when the book page is live) |

| related_slugs | Up to 3 related articles |

| seo_title, meta_description | Page title and meta description for this article |

Display requests (needed for the HTML body to look right)

  1. Render `body_html` as HTML (sanitized), with `<h2>` styled like the existing sub-section heading, normal paragraph spacing, and bullets as a proper list with wrapped lines aligned to the text.
  2. Show cover images without cutting important parts: `object-fit: cover` with `object-position: center` is fine for these text-free covers.
  3. Use each article's own title, description and social_image in the page head (og: tags), ideally prerendered so LinkedIn and WhatsApp previews show the article.

After import

  • Article 1 ("Marketing Is Not Failing. It Is Misplaced.") already exists: please update it from this file rather than creating a duplicate.
  • Delete any test articles.
  • Send the author a link to the blog page to check.
